nameStory: The Lattice Orbweaver gets its name from the intricate geometric pattern on its back that resembles a lattice or crosshatch design. Like looking at a delicate garden trellis, the spider's markings form an interconnected network of lines and shapes. This beautiful "lattice" pattern helps distinguish it from other orbweavers in your garden.
description: The Lattice Orbweaver is a medium-sized spider that builds classic round webs with sticky spiral threads - the quintessential "spider web" most people picture. Like other orbweavers, it has a bulbous abdomen and relatively short legs compared to its body size. These spiders typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch in body length. They're part of the large Araneus genus, which includes many of New England's most common garden spiders.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive lattice or crosshatch pattern on the abdomen that gives this spider its name - the markings form an intricate geometric design that feels almost woven when you examine it closely

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic circular orb webs with sticky spiral capture threads radiating from the center - the silk feels remarkably strong when accidentally walked through

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Has the typical orbweaver build with a rounded, bulbous abdomen that looks almost balloon-like and legs that appear proportionally shorter than those of hunting spiders

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for an orbweaver, with females reaching about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch in body length, not counting the legs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web during evening hours or hides in nearby foliage during the day, connected to the web by a signal thread that vibrates when prey is caught

habitat: Lattice Orbweavers build their webs in gardens, forest edges, and areas with mixed vegetation where they can anchor their circular webs between shrubs, tall grasses, or garden plants. They prefer spots with some protection from wind but enough open space to construct their full orb webs. Look for them in residential areas with landscaping as well as natural woodland clearings and meadow edges.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders emerge and begin establishing territories, building their first webs as the weather warms and flying insects become more active.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are fully grown and most visible in their webs, especially during evening hours when they're actively hunting.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs, with females producing egg sacs that will overwinter. Adults remain active until the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off, but egg sacs overwinter in protected locations like under loose bark or in garden debris, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: Orbweaver spiders like the Lattice Orbweaver actually eat and rebuild their entire web almost every single day, recycling the protein-rich silk by consuming it before spinning a fresh web - it's like having a self-cleaning, renewable hunting trap!
confusionNotes: The Lattice Orbweaver can be confused with other Araneus orbweavers, but the distinctive lattice pattern on the abdomen is the key difference. Remember: "Lattice pattern, Lattice spider" - if you see crosshatch markings that look like a garden trellis, you've found your Lattice Orbweaver rather than the crosses of Cross Orbweavers or the marbling of Marbled Orbweavers.
contextualKnowledge: The Lattice Orbweaver is less commonly encountered than some of its famous relatives like the Cross Orbweaver or Marbled Orbweaver, with only 64 recorded observations in New England. This doesn't necessarily mean it's rare, but rather that it may be overlooked or misidentified due to the challenge of distinguishing between similar Araneus species without close examination of their markings.
compareHints: Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver. While the Shamrock Orbweaver has foliate patterns resembling three-leaf designs, the Lattice Orbweaver's markings are more geometric and grid-like. The lattice pattern is more structured and angular than the varied spotting found on species like the Red-spotted Orbweaver.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
